extracted.intended_audience: researchers and NLP practitioners building annotation schemas and classifiers for grant peer review / peer review analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and applying an annotation schema to label sentences from grant peer review reports according to evaluation criteria (e.g., track record, methods, feasibility, suggestions, rationale) for training classifiers and analysing peer review. Includes mapping to SNSF evaluation criteria and example sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s scientific track record and expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific qualifications of each applicant, in particular the track record and the expertise to carry out the research project, based on their entire research output beyond research publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used by SNSF evaluators to assess whether applicants have the necessary experience and prior accomplishments to execute the project. Example signals: statements about prior work, leadership in the field, prior relevant publications, demonstrated interdisciplinary competence (see example sentences in F.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific relevance, originality and topicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and to what extent the proposed project: - is relevant and increasing knowledge and coherence or has the potential to develop approaches and methods in the discipline or beyond - uses a theoretical/methodical approach that is original and offers unexpected or novel combinations of familiar aspects or focuses on a question that has been neglected by researchers - is of current interest
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators note novelty, topical importance, and potential to advance the field; cues include explicit claims of originality, novelty, or topical relevance (see F.2 example sentences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and to what extent the chosen methods are suited to answering the questions set out in the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments focus on match between methods and research questions, state-of-the-art techniques, clarity and robustness of methodological plans. Example indicators: mentions of specific methods (CNN, Random Forest), statements that methods are appropriate, state-of-the-art, or robust (see F.3 and F.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether and to what extent the project is feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluators judge feasibility based on scope, defined aims, preliminary data, applicant expertise, and resource availability. Typical markers: 'feasible', 'objectives are achievable', references to preliminary/existing work supporting feasibility (see F.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader impact (for 'Use‑Inspired Proposals' only)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project’s broader impact outside science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies only to use-inspired proposals; reviewers consider potential societal, industrial, or policy impact beyond academia. This category was trialed in annotations as 'Impact beyond' / 'Impact beyond Academia'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall comment / Summary of reasons for overall rating
rubrics_metrics.description: Summary of the main reasons for the overall rating by pointing out the strengths and weaknesses of the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A high-level evaluative paragraph that synthesizes strengths and weaknesses and justifies the numeric/qualitative rating; often contains multiple category signals (e.g., track record + methods + feasibility).

rubrics_metrics.name: Track Record (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'criterion track record' used to label sentences addressing applicants' past accomplishments and suitability based on previous output.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: explicit mentions of applicants' expertise, publications, accomplishments, productivity, leadership in subfields (see F.1). Frequently appears as concrete praise of CV, publication record, or demonstrations of prior relevant work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevance, Originality, Topicality (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'criterion relevance originality topicality' used for sentences about novelty, relevance, and topical importance of the proposed work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences that explicitly state the project is relevant, original, novel, timely, or topical. Examples and phrasings given in F.2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'criterion suitability' for sentences that assess whether chosen approaches, techniques, and designs are appropriate for the research aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers statements like 'methods are suitable', 'methodological approach convincing', or listings of appropriate techniques; examples in F.3 and F.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'criterion feasibility' for sentences explicitly about project achievability and realistic scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences declaring the project feasible or giving reasons for feasibility (preliminary data, defined aims, applicant experience). Examples in F.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'candidate other' / 'candidate' capturing general evaluative sentences about the applicant(s) (qualifications, fit, competence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes broader statements about the applicants' combined expertise, suitability to carry out the program, or domain-relevant background (examples in F.7).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant: Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'candidate quantity' for sentences that quantify applicant productivity (publication counts, h-index, patents, authorship positions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: counts of publications, h-index statements, numbers of patents—used to capture quantitative indicators of productivity (see F.8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'proposal general' for sentences assessing the overall quality, rationale, novelty, and timeliness of the proposal itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label high-level evaluative statements about the proposal's rationale, clarity, novelty, and potential impact (examples in F.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'proposal method' (often shown as 'Methods') for sentences that evaluate specific methodological choices and their articulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covers statements about whether methods are appropriate, established, well-articulated, or solid; examples in F.6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positive statement (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'positive' marking sentences that express praise, strengths, or supportive evaluation of applicant/proposal/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical cues: 'strengths of this proposal are...', 'highly compelling', 'outstanding contributions' (examples in F.9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative statement (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'negative' marking sentences that express criticism, weaknesses, or concerns about applicant/proposal/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical cues: spelling mistakes, inadequate literature review, questionable generalizability, methodological gaps (examples in F.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'suggestion' for sentences offering concrete recommendations or proposed improvements to the proposal or methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label sentences that give actionable advice (e.g., methodological changes, additional experiments, clarifications). Examples are present across coding rounds though specific F-section examples are not enumerated in the chunk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale (annotation category)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'rationale' capturing sentences that provide argumentation, justification, or sub-stantiation for an evaluative claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This category proved difficult for annotators: it identifies the presence of an argument/substantiation rather than just an opinion. Annotators distinguish 'Rationale', 'Rationale: Context', and combinations. Prevalence and inter-annotator agreement vary; see discussion in A9–A16 and Table A8 for difficulty and classifier performance. Use cases: sentences that explain why a claim is made, offering evidence or reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale: Context / Rationale and Context
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation variants that mark when a rationale is dependent on surrounding sentences or when context is necessary to identify the reasoned support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used when a sentence by itself is ambiguous but, together with preceding/following sentences, constitutes a rationale. The paper tests models using surrounding sentences to improve detection (see E.2 and Table A8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit evaluation (trialed category)
rubrics_metrics.description: A codebook category ('Implicit Evaluation') trialed in annotation rounds to capture evaluations that are not explicit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The manuscript notes this category was trialed in some rounds but not used in the three main annotation rounds; treat as experimental/rare. Label if evaluation is implied without explicit evaluative wording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact beyond / Impact beyond Academia
rubrics_metrics.description: Annotation codebook category 'impact beyond' capturing sentences about the proposal's effects outside academia (societal, policy, industrial impact).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to identify statements that claim or discuss broader societal/industrial impact; was trialed and included in some coding rounds (see Table A1 and A8).
